name: hazard-screening-rules
licence: CC0-1.0 (public domain dedication) — first-party SMARTS and explanations, ported from Chemclaw3's `chemclaw.science.safety`, which is MIT-licensed content of the same owner. The hazard *concepts* are published science attributed per row (see retrieved_from); the patterns and the flag text encoding them were written in that repository. Same basis as this server's `genotox` table, and deliberately not the basis its `ich_q3c`/`ich_q3d` tables use — those transcribe figures out of a guideline and carry that guideline's terms instead.
retrieved_from: Ported byte-for-byte from Chemclaw3's `src/chemclaw/science/safety/rules.yaml` (D-080, D-086), where it was written as first-party content: eleven structural SMARTS and (as of 0.2.0) six pairwise-incompatibility SMARTS, each composed in that repository against a named source rather than copied out of one. The sources every rule cites are Bretherick's Handbook of Reactive Chemical Hazards, 8th ed. (azides, diazonium salts, peroxides, nitrate esters, polynitroaryl compounds, perchlorates, hydrazines, N-haloamines, oxidant/reductant mixtures, peroxide/ketone, metal hydrides); Bräse et al., Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2005, 44, 5188; Green et al., Org. Process Res. Dev. 2020, 24, 67; Buckley et al., Org. Process Res. Dev. 2021, 25, 587; and Peet & Weber, Chem. Eng. News 1988, 66(31), 2. Nothing is fetched at runtime and no address here is read by any code.
description: Seventeen deterministic hazard-screening rules — eleven structural motifs (organic, non-carbon and acyl azides, diazo, diazonium, peroxide, nitrate ester, polynitroaromatic, perchlorate, hydrazine, N-halamine) and six pairwise incompatibilities checked across a reaction's components — each with a severity, an explanation written for the person reading the flag, and the literature citation it rests on. The licence was carried as UNRESOLVED through the port and is now settled as first-party: the file cites a source per rule and reproduces none of them. Bretherick's and the four cited papers are prose; they contain no SMARTS, and the patterns here were written — and debugged — in Chemclaw3, which the `peroxide` rule shows plainly (it carries an in-repo fix for `[OX1-]`, because the two-coordinate-only pattern screened sodium peroxide clean — and 0.2.0 carries that same fix into `peroxide-with-ketone`, whose arm the first one had missed). The facts themselves — that an organic azide is shock-sensitive — are not copyrightable subject matter. ADVISORY ONLY: a match is a structural alert for a human to assess, never a hazard assessment, and an empty result means no rule in this table matched — never that the chemistry is safe.
